stories.title: Thunderbird fixes password exposure during Exchange setup
stories.summary: Mozilla’s October 20 advisory identifies Thunderbird 153.5.1 as a high-impact security update. During Exchange account setup, an AutoDiscover request sent over unencrypted HTTP incorrectly included the credentials entered by the user, allowing a network attacker to obtain the password. Another fix addresses incoming XMPP requests that could trigger outgoing chat commands, including messages or contact-setting changes, without user interaction. That vulnerability affects XMPP chat accounts specifically. Malformed authentication challenges from malicious POP3 or SMTP servers could also expose uninitialized memory through NTLM responses or crash the application. These are distinct exposures with different configuration requirements, rather than a claim that simply reading any email compromises an account. Users on this release branch should install the patched version and confirm the update after restarting. The advisory does not establish that these vulnerabilities were exploited against particular users.

stories.title: Coroners report 239 drug-toxicity deaths in July and August
stories.summary: The province’s October 14 bulletin reports preliminary counts of 113 deaths from unregulated drug toxicity in July and 126 in August. Vancouver Coastal and Fraser health authorities each recorded 68 deaths across those two months. Together, those authorities account for 54% of the province’s reported drug-toxicity deaths so far in 2026. People aged 30–59 account for 69% of this year’s deaths, and males account for 76%. The geographic distinction matters: Vancouver Coastal’s figure covers a health authority and cannot be treated as a City of Vancouver count. This release adds newly checked public-health information to the edition, although the deaths occurred during summer. The findings remain preliminary and may be revised as investigations proceed.

stories.title: Improved confidence meets weaker spending intentions
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada’s October 19 consumer survey supplies a household counterpart to yesterday’s business coverage. Respondents reported better financial health, citing financial-asset gains and greater confidence in the labour market. Yet spending plans weakened from already subdued levels as high prices and uncertainty continued to weigh on consumers. Labour-market perceptions improved slightly overall but remained below the survey average; perceptions deteriorated among workers in sectors where AI poses greater task-replacement risks. Long-term inflation expectations rose toward elevated shorter-term expectations. The online survey ran August 5–27, with roughly three-quarters of responses collected before the August 21 breakdown in Canada–US trade talks. Follow-up interviews continued into September. These findings measure perceptions and intentions, rather than actual consumption or inflation: feeling financially stronger did not automatically translate into willingness to spend.

meetups.description: The organizer verifies registration, venue and agenda.
